description: Building, joining, splitting, searching, comparing and formatting text in MATLAB, covering both the modern string array type and the older character vector and cell-array-of-char conventions, plus the regular expression engine and the numeric-to-text conversion functions.

tools.name: strings
tools.description: Preallocates a string array whose elements are all the empty string "". Use it before a loop that fills text element by element, exactly as `zeros` is used for numbers. The result is a string array, not a cell array, so it supports the full set of elementwise string functions.
tools.usage:
str = strings
str = strings(n)
str = strings(sz1, ..., szN)
tools.notes: The empty string "" is not the same as the missing string; use `string(missing)` or `strings(n)` plus assignment of `missing` when you need missing values.

tools.name: strlength
tools.description: Returns the number of characters in each element of a string array, character vector or cell array of character vectors. Use it instead of `numel` or `length` for text, since those report the element count of a string array rather than the text length. Missing string elements return NaN.
tools.usage: L = strlength(str)

parameters.name: str
parameters.description: String array, character vector or cell array of character vectors.

tools.notes: `length("hello")` returns 1 because a string scalar is a single element; this trips up people coming from other languages. Use `strlength(s)==0` to test for an empty string.

tools.name: cellstr
tools.description: Converts a character matrix or string array into a cell array of character vectors, removing the trailing space padding that character matrices carry. Use it when interfacing with functions and file formats that expect cellstr, such as legacy APIs and some table variable names. The inverse conversion is `char` or `string`.
tools.usage:
C = cellstr(A)
C = cellstr(A, dateFmt)

parameters.name: A
parameters.description: Character array, string array, or datetime/duration array.

tools.example:
M = char('red', 'green', 'blue');
size(M)
C = cellstr(M)
cellfun(@numel, C)
cellstr(["a"; "bb"])
tools.notes: cellstr strips only trailing whitespace, not leading. For new code, string arrays are preferred over cellstr, but many older functions still return or require cell arrays of character vectors.

tools.name: strcat
tools.description: Concatenates text horizontally, operating elementwise over arrays so that corresponding elements are joined. Its one notorious quirk is that trailing whitespace is removed from character vector inputs but preserved for string and cell inputs. For string arrays, the + operator is usually clearer.
tools.usage: s = strcat(s1, ..., sN)

parameters.name: s1,...,sN
parameters.description: Character vectors, string arrays or cell arrays of character vectors.

tools.notes: strcat('Hello',' ','World') yields 'HelloWorld' because the trailing space in the char input is stripped; use [ ] concatenation, string arrays or `append` to keep it.

tools.name: strjoin
tools.description: Joins the elements of a string array or cell array of character vectors into a single piece of text, separated by a delimiter. Use it to build comma-separated lists, file paths and SQL-style clauses from a list of pieces. The delimiter may be a single string or a vector of per-gap delimiters.
tools.usage:
str = strjoin(C)
str = strjoin(C, delimiter)

parameters.name: C
parameters.description: String array or cell array of character vectors.

parameters.name: delimiter
parameters.description: Separator text, or a cell/string array with one fewer element than C.

tools.notes: `join` is the newer, more flexible function that also works along a chosen dimension of a multidimensional string array. strjoin requires a vector input.

tools.name: strsplit
tools.description: Splits a character vector or string at delimiters, returning a cell array of the pieces. Multiple delimiters can be supplied and consecutive delimiters can optionally be collapsed. Use it for parsing simple delimited records when `split` or `textscan` would be overkill.
tools.usage:
C = strsplit(str)
C = strsplit(str, delimiter)
[C, matches] = strsplit(___)
C = strsplit(___, Name, Value)

parameters.name: delimiter
parameters.description: Delimiter text, or a cell array of several delimiters.

parameters.name: 'CollapseDelimiters'
parameters.description: true (default) treats runs of delimiters as one.

tools.example:
strsplit('a,b,,c', ',')
strsplit('a,b,,c', ',', 'CollapseDelimiters', false)
strsplit('one1two22three', '\d+', 'DelimiterType', 'RegularExpression')
strsplit('a b  c')
tools.notes: strsplit always returns a cell array even for string input; `split` returns a string array and handles arrays of inputs, so it is preferred in new code.

tools.name: split
tools.description: Splits string array elements at delimiters, producing a string array where each piece occupies its own element along a chosen dimension. All elements must split into the same number of pieces unless you split a scalar. Use it for parsing structured text such as dates, paths or CSV fields into columns.
tools.usage:
C = split(str)
C = split(str, delimiter)
C = split(str, delimiter, dim)
[C, matches] = split(___)

parameters.name: str
parameters.description: String array, character vector or cellstr.

parameters.name: delimiter
parameters.description: One or more delimiters; whitespace by default.

parameters.name: dim
parameters.description: Dimension along which the pieces are laid out.

tools.example:
split("2025-03-14", "-")
parts = split(["a,b"; "c,d"], ",")
size(parts)
split("one two three")
[p, d] = split("x1y2z", ["1" "2"]);
tools.notes: Splitting an array whose elements yield different numbers of pieces is an error; use `splitlines` or a loop with `strsplit` for ragged data. `splitlines` splits specifically at newline characters.

tools.name: join
tools.description: Combines the elements of a string array into fewer elements by joining along a dimension with a delimiter. It is the inverse of `split` and works on multidimensional arrays, unlike `strjoin`. Use it to reassemble parsed fields and to build one line of text per row of a string matrix.
tools.usage:
newStr = join(str)
newStr = join(str, delimiter)
newStr = join(str, delimiter, dim)

parameters.name: str
parameters.description: String array or cellstr to join.

tools.notes: For tables, `join` means a database-style join instead; the two functions are distinguished by the class of the first input.

tools.name: strrep
tools.description: Replaces every occurrence of a substring with another substring, operating elementwise on arrays of text. It performs plain literal substitution with no pattern interpretation, which makes it fast and predictable. Use `regexprep` when you need patterns, and `replace` for the modern string-oriented equivalent.
tools.usage: newStr = strrep(str, old, new)
tools.notes: Replacement scans left to right without rescanning, so strrep('aaa','aa','b') gives 'ba'. Special regex characters are treated literally, which is exactly what you want for path separators.

tools.name: replace
tools.description: Replaces occurrences of one or more substrings in string arrays, accepting vectors of search and replacement text so several substitutions happen in a single pass. It also accepts pattern objects built with the pattern-matching functions. Use it as the string-array-friendly successor to `strrep`.
tools.usage: newStr = replace(str, old, new)

parameters.name: str
parameters.description: String array, character vector or cellstr.

parameters.name: old
parameters.description: Text or array of texts to find, or a pattern object.

parameters.name: new
parameters.description: Replacement text, scalar or matching the size of old.

tools.example:
replace("the quick fox", ["quick" "fox"], ["slow" "dog"])
replace(["a1"; "b2"], digitsPattern, "#")
replace("2025-03-14", "-", "/")
tools.notes: Each part of the input is replaced at most once per pass, so replacements cannot cascade into each other. `replaceBetween` substitutes the text between two delimiters.

tools.name: insertAfter
tools.description: Inserts text after a specified substring, position or pattern in each element of a string array. Use it to add suffixes, annotate identifiers, and inject separators without manual index arithmetic. The companion `insertBefore` inserts on the other side.
tools.usage:
newStr = insertAfter(str, pat, newText)
newStr = insertAfter(str, pos, newText)

parameters.name: pat
parameters.description: Substring or pattern after which to insert.

parameters.name: pos
parameters.description: Numeric position after which to insert.

tools.notes: When the pattern occurs several times, insertion happens after every occurrence. If the pattern is absent, the text is returned unchanged rather than erroring.

tools.name: extractBefore
tools.description: Returns the substring that appears before a given position, substring or pattern. Use it to strip file extensions, take the key part of a key=value pair, and truncate at a marker. It returns missing when the pattern is not found, which is easy to test with `ismissing`.
tools.usage:
newStr = extractBefore(str, pat)
newStr = extractBefore(str, pos)

parameters.name: pat
parameters.description: Substring or pattern marking the end.

parameters.name: pos
parameters.description: Numeric position before which to extract.

tools.notes: With multiple occurrences of the pattern, extraction stops at the first one. Use `fileparts` rather than string surgery when you are actually parsing file names.

tools.name: extractAfter
tools.description: Returns the substring that appears after a given position, substring or pattern. Use it to take file extensions, values from key=value pairs, and the tail of a delimited record. Like `extractBefore` it returns missing when the pattern does not occur.
tools.usage:
newStr = extractAfter(str, pat)
newStr = extractAfter(str, pos)

parameters.name: pat
parameters.description: Substring or pattern marking the start.

parameters.name: pos
parameters.description: Numeric position after which to extract.

tools.notes: Extraction starts after the first occurrence of the pattern, so 'a-b-c' with delimiter '-' yields 'b-c'. Combine with `extractBefore` to take a middle section, or use `extractBetween`.

tools.name: extractBetween
tools.description: Extracts the substring lying between two delimiters or two positions, optionally including the boundaries themselves. Use it to pull values out of tagged text, to read fields between brackets, and to take fixed-width slices. When several matches exist it returns them all in a string array.
tools.usage:
newStr = extractBetween(str, startPat, endPat)
newStr = extractBetween(str, startPos, endPos)
newStr = extractBetween(___, 'Boundaries', bounds)
tools.notes: For genuinely structured markup use `readstruct`, `xmlread` or `jsondecode` rather than string extraction. Multiple matches return a multi-element string array, so the output size can surprise you.

tools.name: contains
tools.description: Tests whether each element of a text array contains a given substring or pattern, returning a logical array. Use it for filtering lists of file names, log lines and labels. Several search terms can be supplied at once, in which case a match against any of them counts.
tools.usage:
TF = contains(str, pat)
TF = contains(str, pat, 'IgnoreCase', true)

parameters.name: pat
parameters.description: Substring, array of substrings, or pattern object.

tools.example:
files = ["a.mat"; "b.txt"; "c.mat"];
files(contains(files, ".mat"))
contains("Hello World", "world", 'IgnoreCase', true)
contains(["abc" "xyz"], ["a" "z"])
tools.notes: contains does substring matching, not pattern matching, unless you pass a pattern object. Use `matches` to test whether the whole text equals the pattern.

tools.name: startsWith
tools.description: Tests whether each element of a text array begins with a given substring or pattern. Use it for prefix filtering such as selecting variables by naming convention or files by a leading tag. Multiple prefixes can be tested in a single call.
tools.usage:
TF = startsWith(str, pat)
TF = startsWith(str, pat, 'IgnoreCase', true)

parameters.name: pat
parameters.description: Prefix text, array of prefixes, or pattern object.

tools.notes: For path prefixes on Windows, remember that comparison is case sensitive by default even though the file system is not.

tools.name: endsWith
tools.description: Tests whether each element of a text array ends with a given substring or pattern. Use it to select files by extension, to detect terminated lines and to validate suffix conventions. Like `startsWith` it accepts several candidate suffixes.
tools.usage:
TF = endsWith(str, pat)
TF = endsWith(str, pat, 'IgnoreCase', true)

parameters.name: pat
parameters.description: Suffix text, array of suffixes, or pattern object.

tools.example:
files = ["a.csv"; "b.mat"; "c.CSV"];
files(endsWith(files, ".csv", 'IgnoreCase', true))
endsWith("line\n", newline)
endsWith(["ab" "cd"], "d")
tools.notes: For file extension tests, `fileparts` is more robust because it handles names containing several dots correctly.

tools.name: count
tools.description: Counts how many times a substring or pattern occurs in each element of a text array. Use it for frequency analysis, for validating delimiter counts before parsing, and for quick checks on log content. It counts non-overlapping occurrences scanning left to right.
tools.usage:
A = count(str, pat)
A = count(str, pat, 'IgnoreCase', true)

parameters.name: pat
parameters.description: Substring, array of substrings, or pattern object.

tools.notes: Overlapping occurrences are not counted twice, so count('aaa','aa') is 1. With an array of patterns, the counts of all patterns are summed.

tools.name: strfind
tools.description: Returns the starting indices of every occurrence of a substring, including overlapping ones. Use it when you need positions rather than a yes/no answer, for example to locate all delimiters before slicing. It returns an empty array when there is no match.
tools.usage:
k = strfind(str, pat)
k = strfind(str, pat, 'ForceCellOutput', true)

parameters.name: str
parameters.description: Text to search; an array produces a cell array of index vectors.

tools.notes: Unlike `count`, strfind reports overlapping matches. For pattern-based positions use the second and third outputs of `regexp`.

tools.name: strcmp
tools.description: Compares text for exact equality, returning a logical array and handling cell arrays and string arrays elementwise. It is the safe way to compare character vectors, because == on char arrays compares character by character and errors when lengths differ. Use `strcmpi` for case-insensitive comparison.
tools.usage: tf = strcmp(s1, s2)

parameters.name: s1, s2
parameters.description: Character vectors, string arrays or cell arrays of character vectors.

tools.notes: strcmp compares whole strings and returns one logical per element, whereas == on char vectors of equal length compares each character. For string arrays, == works elementwise and is equivalent to strcmp.

tools.name: strcmpi
tools.description: Compares text for equality while ignoring case, returning logical results elementwise over arrays. Use it for user input handling, option name matching and any comparison where capitalization is not significant. It has the same argument rules as `strcmp`.
tools.usage: tf = strcmpi(s1, s2)

parameters.name: s1, s2
parameters.description: Character vectors, string arrays or cell arrays of character vectors.

tools.example:
strcmpi('MATLAB', 'matlab')
strcmpi({'Yes','No','yes'}, 'YES')
opt = 'Linear';
if strcmpi(opt, 'linear'), disp('linear selected'), end
tools.notes: Case folding uses simple per-character rules and is not locale-aware for every alphabet. `validatestring` performs case-insensitive partial matching against a list of valid options.

tools.name: strncmp
tools.description: Compares only the first n characters of two pieces of text for equality. Use it for prefix matching of option names, for grouping identifiers by a leading code, and for abbreviation handling. `strncmpi` is the case-insensitive variant.
tools.usage: tf = strncmp(s1, s2, n)

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: Number of leading characters to compare.

tools.notes: If either input is shorter than n, the comparison returns false rather than erroring. `startsWith` is usually clearer for prefix tests in new code.

tools.name: regexp
tools.description: Matches a regular expression against text and returns any combination of start indices, end indices, matched text, token captures, named tokens and split pieces. It supports lookahead, lookbehind, lazy quantifiers, named capture groups and dynamic expressions. Use it for parsing semi-structured text that simple substring functions cannot handle.
tools.usage:
startIndex = regexp(str, expression)
[tok, mat] = regexp(str, expression, 'tokens', 'match')
out = regexp(str, expression, outkey)
out = regexp(str, expression, 'names')
out = regexp(str, expression, 'once')

parameters.name: 'once'
parameters.description: Return only the first match, unwrapped from its cell.

tools.notes: In MATLAB, backslashes inside single-quoted patterns are literal, so no double escaping is needed. Requesting 'once' returns a char vector instead of a nested cell, which usually simplifies downstream code.

tools.name: regexpi
tools.description: Performs the same regular expression matching as `regexp` but ignores case by default. Use it when the source text has inconsistent capitalization, such as log files or user-entered data. All the output keywords and options of regexp are available.
tools.usage:
startIndex = regexpi(str, expression)
out = regexpi(str, expression, outkey)
tools.notes: You can achieve the same effect with `regexp(..., 'ignorecase')`; regexpi is just a shorthand. Case-insensitive matching is slower for very large inputs.

tools.name: regexprep
tools.description: Replaces text that matches a regular expression, with support for capture group references such as $1 in the replacement and for dynamic expressions that evaluate MATLAB code. Use it for reformatting, normalizing whitespace, rewriting identifiers and cleaning data. Options control case sensitivity, how many occurrences are replaced and multiline behaviour.
tools.usage:
newStr = regexprep(str, expression, replace)
newStr = regexprep(___, options)

parameters.name: replace
parameters.description: Replacement text; $1, $2 refer to capture groups, ${...} evaluates an expression.

parameters.name: N
parameters.description: A numeric option replaces only the Nth occurrence.

tools.notes: The `${...}` dynamic form executes MATLAB code for every match, so never build it from untrusted input. Literal dollar signs in the replacement must be escaped as `$$`.

tools.name: sprintf
tools.description: Formats data into text using C-style conversion specifications, returning the result as a character vector rather than printing it. The format string is reapplied cyclically until all inputs are consumed, which is how you format a whole vector in one call. Use it for building messages, file names and formatted report lines.
tools.usage:
str = sprintf(formatSpec, A1, ..., An)
str = sprintf(literalText)

parameters.name: formatSpec
parameters.description: Format string with %d, %f, %e, %g, %s, %c and escape sequences such as \n and \t.

parameters.name: A1,...,An
parameters.description: Values to format; arrays are consumed elementwise.

tools.example:
sprintf('%5.2f', pi)
sprintf('%d, ', [1 2 3])
sprintf('%s scored %d\n', 'Ann', 91)
name = sprintf('run_%03d.mat', 7)
sprintf('%-10s|', 'left')
tools.notes: Escape sequences such as \n are interpreted in single-quoted format strings here, unlike in ordinary MATLAB char literals. `fprintf` writes the same formatting to the command window or a file, and `compose` returns a string array with one element per row of input.

tools.name: num2str
tools.description: Converts a numeric array to a character array for display, with optional precision or an explicit format string. Matrices become multi-row character arrays with columns aligned. Use it for labels, titles and messages; for exact round-trippable text use `mat2str` or `sprintf` with enough digits.
tools.usage:
s = num2str(A)
s = num2str(A, precision)
s = num2str(A, formatSpec)
tools.example:
num2str(pi)
num2str(pi, 10)
num2str([1 2; 3 4])
title(['Result: ' num2str(3.14159, '%0.2f')])
num2str(1e-10)
tools.notes: The default gives about five significant digits, which silently loses precision. For string arrays, `string(A)` gives a shorter and more faithful conversion.

tools.name: str2num
tools.description: Converts text to a number by evaluating it as a MATLAB expression, which means it can parse matrix literals such as '[1 2; 3 4]'. Because it uses `eval`, it executes arbitrary code and must never be used on untrusted input. Prefer `str2double` for plain numbers.
tools.usage:
X = str2num(chr)
[X, tf] = str2num(chr)

parameters.name: chr
parameters.description: Character vector holding a numeric expression.

tools.example:
str2num('[1 2 3]')
str2num('2+3')
[v, ok] = str2num('not a number');
ok
str2double('3.14')
tools.notes: str2num('system(''rm -rf /'')') would execute that command, so treat it as dangerous. The second output tells you whether the conversion succeeded.

tools.name: str2double
tools.description: Converts text to a double-precision number without evaluating it as code, returning NaN for anything that does not parse. It works elementwise on string arrays and cell arrays, which makes it ideal for converting whole columns of imported text. It understands scientific notation, leading signs, Inf and NaN.
tools.usage: X = str2double(str)

parameters.name: str
parameters.description: String array, character vector or cell array of character vectors.

tools.notes: It does not accept thousands separators or currency symbols; strip those first with `regexprep`. Returning NaN rather than erroring makes it easy to detect bad records with `isnan`.

tools.name: mat2str
tools.description: Converts a matrix to a character vector containing a MATLAB literal that reproduces it exactly, including brackets and semicolons. Use it for logging exact values, generating code and writing reproducible test cases. By default it uses 15 significant digits so that round-tripping through `str2num` is lossless.
tools.usage:
str = mat2str(A)
str = mat2str(A, n)
str = mat2str(A, 'class')

parameters.name: 'class'
parameters.description: Include the class name so the literal reconstructs the exact type.

tools.notes: mat2str handles only 2-D arrays. For display purposes `num2str` is more compact but not round-trippable.

tools.name: lower
tools.description: Converts text to lowercase, leaving non-letter characters unchanged. Use it to normalize identifiers, file extensions and user input before comparison or as dictionary keys. It works elementwise on string arrays, character arrays and cell arrays of character vectors.
tools.usage: newStr = lower(str)
tools.example:
lower('MATLAB')
lower(["ABC"; "DeF"])
keys = lower({'Name','AGE'})
strcmp(lower(a), lower(b))
tools.notes: For a direct case-insensitive comparison, `strcmpi` avoids creating temporary lowercase copies. Case conversion follows simple Unicode rules and is not locale-specific.

tools.name: upper
tools.description: Converts text to uppercase, leaving non-letter characters unchanged. Use it for display headings, for normalizing codes such as country or currency abbreviations, and for canonical keys. It is the counterpart of `lower` and accepts the same input types.
tools.usage: newStr = upper(str)
tools.example:
upper('matlab')
upper(["abc"; "dEf"])
code = upper(strtrim(' usd '))
upper("file.txt")
tools.notes: Uppercasing and then lowercasing is not always the identity for every alphabet, so do not rely on round-tripping case conversions.

tools.name: strtrim
tools.description: Removes leading and trailing whitespace, including spaces, tabs and other nonprinting characters, from each element of a text array. Use it to clean up values read from files, forms and user input before comparison. Interior whitespace is left untouched.
tools.usage: newStr = strtrim(str)
tools.example:
strtrim('   padded   ')
strtrim(["  a "; " b  "])
strtrim(sprintf('\t tabbed \n'))
strlength(strtrim("  x  "))
tools.notes: `strip` is the more flexible modern alternative that can trim only one side or trim a specified character. `deblank` removes trailing whitespace only.

tools.name: strip
tools.description: Removes leading, trailing or both leading and trailing characters from text, defaulting to whitespace but accepting any single character to strip. Use it to remove quotation marks, padding characters or leading zeros from imported fields. It operates elementwise on string arrays and cell arrays.
tools.usage:
newStr = strip(str)
newStr = strip(str, side)
newStr = strip(str, pad)
newStr = strip(str, side, pad)

parameters.name: pad
parameters.description: Character to remove; whitespace by default.

tools.notes: strip removes only one character type at a time, not a set. For arbitrary patterns use `regexprep` with anchors.

tools.name: pad
tools.description: Pads text to a common length, either the longest element or an explicit width, adding characters on the left, right or both sides. Use it to align columns in fixed-width reports and to build tabular console output. The padding character defaults to a space.
tools.usage:
newStr = pad(str)
newStr = pad(str, numChars)
newStr = pad(str, side)
newStr = pad(str, numChars, side, padCharacter)

parameters.name: numChars
parameters.description: Target width; defaults to the longest element.

tools.notes: Padding produces text of equal length, which is what `char` does implicitly when building a character matrix. For numeric zero padding, `sprintf('%03d', n)` is more direct.

tools.name: compose
tools.description: Formats data into a string array using the same conversion specifications as `sprintf`, but produces one string element per row of the input rather than one long character vector. Use it to build arrays of labels, file names and formatted values for tables or plots. The format is applied cyclically to the columns of each row.
tools.usage:
str = compose(formatSpec, A)
str = compose(formatSpec, A1, ..., An)
str = compose(txt)

parameters.name: A1,...,An
parameters.description: Data to format; each row produces one output element.

tools.example:
compose('%d items', [1; 2; 3])
compose('%s = %5.2f', ["a"; "b"], [1.5; 2.25])
files = compose('run_%03d.mat', (1:3)')
sprintf('%d items', [1; 2; 3])
tools.notes: compose returns a string array while sprintf concatenates everything into one character vector, which is the key difference when generating lists. Escape sequences are interpreted as in sprintf.

tools.name: blanks
tools.description: Creates a character vector consisting of n space characters. Use it to build fixed-width output by hand, to indent generated text, and to separate fields in character matrices. It is a small helper that makes alignment code more readable.
tools.usage: chr = blanks(n)
tools.example:
['[' blanks(5) ']']
indent = blanks(4);
disp([indent 'nested line'])
numel(blanks(3))
tools.notes: `pad` and `sprintf` field widths are usually better for alignment because they adapt to the content length.

tools.name: deblank
tools.description: Removes trailing whitespace and null characters from text, leaving leading whitespace intact. Use it when reading fixed-width records or character matrices where every row is space-padded to the same length. For both ends, use `strtrim` instead.
tools.usage: newStr = deblank(str)

parameters.name: str
parameters.description: Character array, string array or cell array of character vectors.

tools.example:
['[' deblank('  text   ') ']']
['[' strtrim('  text   ') ']']
M = char('ab', 'cdef');
deblank(M(1,:))
tools.notes: Extracting a row from a character matrix always brings the padding with it, which is why deblank or strtrim is needed after indexing such matrices.
